title: Generic Methods, Bounds and Wildcards
learningObjectives: Declare generic methods with type parameters before return types
Restrict generic types with bounded type parameter declarations
Read producer values safely using extends wildcards
Add consumer values safely using super wildcards
Explain PECS and the purpose of generic type erasure

understand.concept: Generic methods declare type parameters before the return type. Bounds restrict acceptable types. extends is useful for producers and super for consumers.
understand.whyItMatters: Generic Methods, Bounds and Wildcards helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Generic methods

A generic method declares its own type parameter list before the return type, for example <T> T first(List<T> values). The method's type parameter is inferred from the arguments when possible, or can be supplied explicitly. A method-level type parameter is independent of any type parameter declared by its enclosing class.

## Bounds

An upper bound such as <T extends Number> restricts T to Number or one of its subclasses. This lets the method safely call Number methods such as doubleValue. A type parameter may have multiple bounds; when a class bound is present, it must appear first, followed by interface bounds.

## Wildcard types

List<?> means a list of an unknown element type. It is useful when code only needs operations that do not depend on the element type, such as reading its size. List<? extends Number> is an upper-bounded wildcard: values can be read as Number, but adding an arbitrary Number is not safe because the actual list could be List<Integer> or List<Double>.

List<? super Integer> is a lower-bounded wildcard. It can safely accept Integer values (and subclasses), while values read from it are known only as Object. These rules are often summarized as PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

## Invariance and API design

Even though Integer extends Number, List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>. Wildcards express the safe variance needed by an API without allowing writes that could violate the collection's actual element type.

## Type erasure and limitations

Generic type arguments are erased from most runtime operations. Generic methods and classes therefore cannot generally create T with new T(), use T.class, or create arrays of T. Use a Class<T> token or a carefully designed factory when runtime construction is required.

examples.title: Core concept
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { class NumberTools { <T extends Number> double sum(java.util.List<T> values) { double total=0; for(T value:values) total+=value.doubleValue(); return total; } } NumberTools tools = new NumberTools(); System.out.println(tools.sum(java.util.List.of(2,3,4))); } }
examples.explanation: The method declares <T extends Number>, so its parameter may contain numeric wrapper values and each value can be converted with doubleValue.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { class First { <T> T get(java.util.List<T> values) { return values.get(0); } } System.out.println(new First().get(java.util.List.of("red","blue"))); } }
examples.explanation: The type parameter T is inferred from the supplied list, and the method returns an element with that same compile-time type.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { class Total { double sum(java.util.List<? extends Number> values) { double total=0; for(Number n:values) total+=n.doubleValue(); return total; } } System.out.println(new Total().sum(java.util.List.of(1,2,3))); } }
examples.explanation: List<? extends Number> is a producer of Number values: the method can read them as Number but cannot safely add an Integer.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { class Add { void addOne(java.util.List<? super Integer> values) { values.add(1); } } java.util.List<Number> values = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); new Add().addOne(values); System.out.println(values); } }
examples.explanation: List<? super Integer> is a consumer of Integer values: adding Integer is safe, while a retrieved element has only the known type Object.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { class Show { <T> void show(T value) { System.out.println(value.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } new Show().show("Java"); } }
examples.explanation: The compiler infers the generic method's type argument from the invocation, allowing the returned value to be assigned to the matching reference type.

practise.guidedTask: Write a generic method that returns the first element of List<T>, then write a bounded method that sums List<? extends Number>.
practise.independentTask: Implement a method that copies Integer values into a destination List<? super Integer>. Explain why the wildcard supports adding integers.
hints: Declare method type parameters immediately before the return type, such as <T> T method(...).
Use extends when a structure produces values for reading and super when it consumes values for writing.
Remember that List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>; use a wildcard to express a safe API.
practise.challenge: Create compile-time examples demonstrating extends for reading and super for writing. Explain type erasure at a high level.
